stages.name: Basics
body: One server can only handle so many requests before it slows down or falls over. F5's NGINX documentation describes load balancing across multiple application instances as a common technique for optimising resource utilisation, maximising throughput, reducing latency and improving fault tolerance [[nginx-lb]]. A load balancer is the server that sits in front of a group of backends and spreads incoming requests across them, so no single machine is overwhelmed.

The second job is just as important: availability. F5's glossary says load balancers are used to distribute capacity during peak traffic and to increase reliability of applications [[nginx-glossary]]. HAProxy's guide describes the mechanism: only valid servers are used, and the others are automatically evicted from the load balancing farm [[haproxy-intro]].

Because the load balancer is the invisible facilitator between users and the server group, as the glossary puts it, clients do not need to know how many servers there are [[nginx-glossary]]. You can add or remove backends behind it without clients noticing, which is the foundation for scaling horizontally.

terms.definition: A server that distributes incoming requests across a pool of backends.
The group of backend servers a load balancer sends traffic to.
Handling more load by adding more servers, rather than making one server bigger.
The share of time a service is up and answering requests.
The single front address clients connect to, standing in for the whole pool.

stages.name: How it works
body: When a request arrives, the load balancer picks a backend using a method. NGINX lists algorithms ranging from basic Round Robin to Least Connections, Least Time and hashing-based methods. Least Connections passes a request to the server with the smallest number of active connections [[nginx-lb]].

Not all backends are equal, so a backend can be given a weight. NGINX's example gives one server weight=5 so it receives a larger share of requests than a server with the default weight, and says several methods, including Round Robin, Least Connections and Random, support server weights [[nginx-lb]].

The load balancer only sends traffic to backends it believes are healthy. HAProxy's guide describes health checks: periodic probes to ensure a component is still operational. It says the probes must be representative of the failure, since a ping will not notice that a web server has stopped listening on its port, while a connection to the port will, and a more advanced request can even check that the database it relies on is reachable [[haproxy-intro]].

Load balancing happens at different layers. HAProxy's guide describes a packet-level kind, called layer 4, that is very fast but provides almost no content awareness, and a layer 7 kind, performed by proxies, that reassembles the session and can act on its contents, at the cost of extra processing [[haproxy-intro]]. NGINX documents its HTTP load balancing as Layer 7 and points to separate pages for Layer 4 TCP and UDP balancing [[nginx-lb]].

terms.definition: Sending each new request to the next backend in order, then starting over.
Sending the next request to the backend currently handling the fewest.
A number that gives a stronger backend a larger share of the traffic.
A periodic probe that decides whether a backend is fit to receive traffic.
Layer 4 balances raw connections; layer 7 understands HTTP and can route by path or host.

stages.name: Going deeper
body: Many applications keep per-user state on the server, such as a shopping cart. HAProxy's guide calls the need to send a user's requests to the same server stickiness or persistence and uses the shopping cart as its example [[haproxy-intro]]. F5's glossary makes the same point: in some cases all requests from a client must go to the same server for the duration of a session [[nginx-glossary]].

Stickiness by hashing has a cost. HAProxy's guide notes that if the source address is hashed and divided by the number of available servers, then when one server fails the result changes and all users are suddenly sent to a different server and lose their shopping cart. Its answer is to memorise the chosen target, either in the load balancer's memory, where it may need replicating to other load balancers, or in the client, for example with a cookie [[haproxy-intro]]. Keeping session state outside the backends, in a shared store, is the other common fix, which is one reason caching and shared data stores come later on the map.

A single load balancer is itself a single point of failure unless it is made redundant. HAProxy's guide says it integrates with the VRRP daemon keepalived so a floating virtual IP address can move between balancers, and that its stateless design makes takeover seamless [[haproxy-intro]]. F5's glossary also describes DNS load balancing and global server load balancing, which sends users to the nearest endpoint [[nginx-glossary]]. This is where DNS and load balancing meet: DNS can do a coarse first split, and each balancer does the fine-grained split across backends.

terms.definition: Keeping a given client bound to the same backend across requests. Also called sticky sessions.
Per-user data a server keeps between requests, such as a login or a shopping cart.
Keeping session data in one external store so any backend can serve any user.
A component whose failure takes down the whole system, such as a lone load balancer.

stages.name: In practice and trade-offs
body: Choosing a method is a trade-off. Round robin is simple and even when requests cost about the same, but it ignores that some requests are far heavier than others. Least connections adapts to uneven request costs but needs the balancer to track live state, and NGINX notes that with several worker processes its counters need a shared memory zone to work as expected [[nginx-lb]]. A hash keeps a client on one backend, which helps caches on that backend stay warm, but it rebalances poorly when backends are added or removed, as the HAProxy guide's source-address example shows [[haproxy-intro]].

That last problem, how a hash reshuffles when the pool changes, is exactly what the Consistent Hashing topic solves, which is why it sits right after this one. For now the lesson is that plain hashing by backend count is fragile when the count changes.

Layer 7 balancing enables more than routing. Because it works on the content of requests, it can use a cookie or other element to pick a server, and HAProxy's guide calls that the strongest reason to adopt a layer 7 balancer instead of a layer 4 one [[haproxy-intro]]. Layer 7 balancers are also where retries happen: RFC 9110 says idempotent methods are distinguished because the request can be repeated automatically if a communication failure occurs before the client reads the response [[rfc9110]].

terms.definition: How much work one request takes; uneven costs make simple round robin unfair.
Decrypting HTTPS at the balancer so backends can speak plain HTTP behind it.
A request that has the same effect whether it runs once or twice, so it is safe to retry.

misconceptions.myth: A load balancer just splits traffic evenly.
misconceptions.truth: It also evicts failed backends using health checks, which is half of why it exists [[haproxy-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: Round robin is always the fair choice.
misconceptions.truth: NGINX offers weights and methods such as Least Connections because backends and requests differ [[nginx-lb]].

misconceptions.myth: Sticky sessions are a clean way to scale.
misconceptions.truth: HAProxy's guide notes that hashing the source address loses users' sessions when one server fails; remembering the target, or keeping state outside the backends, avoids that [[haproxy-intro]].

misconceptions.myth: A load balancer removes every single point of failure.
misconceptions.truth: The balancer itself can be one; HAProxy's guide describes running balancers with a floating virtual IP address managed through keepalived [[haproxy-intro]].
